'''Warren Sloan Warren''' is the [[James B. Duke Professor]] of Chemistry and director of the Center for Molecular and Biomolecular Imaging<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cmbi.duke.edu |accessdate=November 10, 2011 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20111008012320/http://www.cmbi.duke.edu/ |archivedate=October 8, 2011 |title=CMBI: The Center for Molecular and Biomolecular Imaging }}</ref> at [[Duke University]]. He is also a professor of physics, Radiology, and Biomedical Engineering at the same institution. Warren is a deputy editor of the open-access journal ''[[Science Advances]]''.[https://www.science.org/content/page/science-advances-editorial-board] He has contributed to the theory of [[Quantum coherence#Quantum coherence|Quantum Coherence]] as well as [[Microscope#Rise of modern light microscopes|nonlinear optical spectroscopy]].

==Scholarship==
Warren began his career in the field of [[Nuclear magnetic resonance|Magnetic Resonance]], where his work contributed to the revised understanding of the interactions between widely separated spins.<ref>Weiss, Peter Ulrich, "Magnetic Whispers", Science News, Vol.159(3), p.42 (2001)</ref>  Warren would go on to exploit these  "Intermolecular Multiple Quantum Coherences",<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cs.duke.edu/~brd/Teaching/Bio/asmb/Papers/NMR/WarrenWarren/iMQC1.pdf |title=Intermolecular Multiple Quantum Coherence in Liquids |publisher=Cs.duke.edu |accessdate=2015-02-26}}</ref> and this work helped lead to the development of new pulse sequences for magnetic resonance imaging with new types of contrast. His work in nonlinear optics developed a range of optical methods which exploit laser pulse shaping to image molecular content, including tissue and paintings.<ref>{{cite web|last=Wade |first=Lizzie |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/3d-imaging-reveals-how-paintings-were-made |title=3D Imaging Reveals How Paintings Were Made &#124; Science/AAAS &#124; News |publisher=News.sciencemag.org |date=2014-01-21 |accessdate=2015-02-26}}</ref>
